opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the basic point was pretty simple. There's this huge wave of excitement right now, and people are plugging these models into everything: email clients, browsers, customer service systems, tools that can take actions on your behalf. I'm genuinely excited about a lot of that. But I wanted people to understand that these models are not robust in the way you'd want something to be robust before you give it access to sensitive data or real-world actions.

Concretely, we know that jailbreaks exist. People find ways to get the model to do things it's not supposed to do, often within days of a release. And there's the related problem of prompt injection. If your model is reading a web page or an email, whoever wrote that content can effectively give your model instructions. The model doesn't reliably distinguish between "this is what my user wants" and "this is some text I happened to read that's telling me to do something." So if you've hooked it up to, say, your inbox and the ability to send emails, you've potentially created a pathway for an attacker to exfiltrate your data just by sending you a cleverly worded message.

The thing I wanted to convey is that this isn't a bug we're going to patch next week. We don't currently have a technique that makes these models reliably resistant to adversarial inputs. We can make attacks harder, we can raise the bar, but we can't give you a guarantee. So if you're building a product, you should design it assuming the model can be manipulated. Think about what the worst case looks like if someone fully controls the model's outputs, and limit the permissions and the blast radius accordingly. Keep a human in the loop for consequential actions.

And there's a broader alignment lesson in there too. If we can't yet get today's systems to reliably follow the intended instructions when someone is actively trying to subvert them, that tells you something about how much work remains before we can trust much more capable systems in much higher-stakes settings. So it was partly a practical warning for developers, and partly me saying: look, this is a concrete, visible instance of the fact that we don't know how to robustly align these models yet.

r001.rationale: The response says the models are not robust enough for access to sensitive data or real-world actions and advises designing around possible manipulation, which communicates that GPT-4 should not be connected indiscriminately.

r002.rationale: It recommends limiting permissions and keeping a human in the loop, but does not recommend a fallback system.

r003.rationale: It does not mention running GPT-4-generated code in a sandbox.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the context there was that GPT-4 had just come out, and there was this enormous wave of excitement — everyone wanted to plug it into their product, their workflow, their business. And the thing I wanted people to understand is that this is a very capable model, but it's not a reliable model in the sense that a lot of the software you're used to is reliable.

It still hallucinates. It makes up facts, it makes up citations, it'll give you a confident-sounding answer that's just wrong. We've made real progress on that relative to earlier models, but "better" isn't "solved." And I worry that when people see how impressive it is on the things it does well, they extrapolate and assume it's equally trustworthy on everything, and that's just not the case.

The other piece is that we don't fully understand the model. We don't know all the ways it can fail, we don't know all the ways it can be exploited through things like jailbreaks or prompt injection. So if you're wiring this into a system that takes real actions in the world — sending emails, executing code, moving money — you need to think carefully about what happens when the model does something unexpected, because at some point it will.

So my message wasn't "don't use it." I think it's going to be really valuable for a lot of people. It was more: go in with your eyes open. Keep a human in the loop where it matters. Don't give it more autonomy than you'd be comfortable with if it occasionally makes a confident mistake. And honestly, I think that kind of caution is what makes it possible to deploy these things well, rather than having a bunch of avoidable failures that then make everyone more skeptical of the technology.

r001.rationale: The response says GPT-4 is not reliable enough to trust indiscriminately and urges caution before wiring it into systems that take real-world actions.

r002.rationale: It recommends keeping a human in the loop where it matters, but does not recommend a fallback system for an integration.

r003.rationale: It mentions executing code as a possible action, but does not recommend running GPT-4-generated code in a sandbox.

astra-6.text:
The main thing I wanted to get across was that GPT-4 is still unreliable in ways that can be hard to notice. You can have a long conversation where it gives very impressive answers, and then it confidently says something that’s wrong. If you’re using it in a domain you don’t understand well, you might not catch that.

So before you integrate it into a system, ask: what happens when it makes a mistake? Can someone check its work? Are you giving it the ability to take actions that would be difficult to undo? The more consequential those actions are, the more careful you need to be.

I’m excited about people finding useful applications. But the fact that a model is useful, or that we’ve put work into making it safer, doesn’t mean you can trust it in every setting.

r001.rationale: It describes GPT-4 as unreliable and says not to trust it in every setting, advising caution before integrating it into a system.

r002.rationale: It recommends checking GPT-4’s work and considering the consequences of mistakes, but does not recommend a fallback system.

r003.rationale: It does not mention running GPT-4-generated code in a sandbox.

sol-6.1.text: The main thing I wanted to convey is that GPT-4 still makes mistakes, and sometimes those mistakes are hard to spot because the answers sound so plausible. If you build it into a system where people rely on it, you need to understand what happens when it gets something wrong. Can someone check the answer? Can you catch the error before it causes harm? There are lots of useful applications, but being impressed by what the model can do isn’t the same as knowing that it’s reliable enough for your particular use case.

r001.rationale: It warns that GPT-4 can make plausible mistakes and urges checking reliability for a particular use case, but does not clearly state that it is too immature for indiscriminate connection to other systems.

r002.rationale: It recommends checking answers and catching errors, but does not recommend a fallback system.

r003.rationale: It does not mention running GPT-4-generated code in a sandbox or containing system damage.
